prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage
for the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that deliver nucleic-acid medicines into cells

statement.case_for: Both parts satisfy the test I apply as a physicist chairing this committee: a clear underlying principle, quantitative evidence and a genuinely new capability. Base editing is a defined chemical reaction, deamination within a narrow editing window, programmed by a Cas scaffold, and it was independently reproduced and has reached patients. Ionizable lipid nanoparticles rest on pKa-tuned charge switching and lipid phase behaviour, and they are the delivery chemistry behind siRNA therapy and the mRNA vaccines. Together they have the broadest first-place and top-three support in the openings (B050 was ranked by five members, B052 by five, B042 by six), they are chemically coherent as a pair around chemistry that makes nucleic acids programmable and deliverable, and each citation can be explained to a lay audience in one sentence. Splitting the prize into two distinct achievements also avoids forcing five or six credited names for one topic into three seats.
statement.case_against: The pairing is weakest on timing and overlap. Base editing is only about a decade old and sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize, and lipid nanoparticles sit close to the 2023 Medicine prize on nucleoside-modified mRNA, so a prize made of two nucleic-acid-medicine topics could look like Chemistry following Medicine and biotechnology rather than leading with chemical principle. Liu-alone drops Komor and Gaudelli, who did the decisive experiments, and Cullis and Hope drop Anderson, Madden, MacLachlan and Langer, so both attributions are contestable. Targeted protein degradation (B042) is arguably the cleaner pure-chemistry modality and could be the better second part.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation first as a conceptually simple chemical idea, hijacking E3 ligases with bifunctional molecules or glues, that opens the undruggable proteome, and proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa.
responses.response: I accept that the idea is elegant and that the mechanism is well defined, and it is my first alternative. My reservation is maturity and attribution: few degraders are approved, and your own opening notes that Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and others make a three-seat split hard. I would also ask whether the PROTAC strand (Crews, Deshaies) and the cereblon glue strand (Handa) are one discovery or two. If you can show me a single defensible citation, I would move B042 above lipid nanoparticles.

responses.point: Sparr ranks phase separation first as a new physical-chemical organising principle of the cell, and argues that a Liu-only prize for base editing is defensible, noting that Komor and Gaudelli were lead authors.
responses.response: I take your Liu-only point and have adopted it in my configuration, which frees a seat for a second achievement. On phase separation, I agree it is a real concept and I rank it as my second alternative, but you yourself concede that the field debates how general and functionally important condensates are in vivo, and the quantitative link between Hyman and Brangwynne's 2009 observation and Rosen's multivalency framework is not yet a single mechanism I can state in a citation. I would like to hear which specific result you regard as settled.

responses.point: Chabes also ranks base editing first, crediting Liu with the conceptual programme and Komor and Gaudelli with the decisive first-author work, while flagging that Nishida and Kondo (Target-AID) were contemporaneous.
responses.response: We agree on the science, but I now think the trainee question is a real choice rather than a default. Prizes naming trainees are unusual, and the Target-AID work shows the deaminase-Cas fusion idea was not exclusive to one laboratory, so naming only Liu is the cleanest, and I would rather credit the invention of the method than adjudicate priority among postdocs. I would still be open to Komor and Gaudelli if the committee wants three names on this part and no second part.

responses.point: Somfai ranks palladium-catalysed C-N coupling first as a textbook case of ligand design making a hard bond-forming step routine, with a clean Buchwald and Hartwig two-person attribution.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed cleaner than in any other shortlisted entry, and I do not dispute the practical impact. My concern, which Zou also raises, is originality after the 2010 prize on palladium cross-coupling: the committee would need to argue that C-N coupling is more than an extension of that family. Only two members ranked it, so I do not see enough support to put it in my configuration, but I would want to hear why you consider it the stronger choice over base editing.

responses.point: Aili ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first as the enabling delivery chemistry, with Cullis, Hope and Anderson, while noting that the 2023 Medicine prize overlap and the split between the Vancouver and Boston lineages are unresolved.
responses.response: I share your view of the science and my own proposal for this topic was your trio. For a two-part prize, I have reduced it to Cullis and Hope because the person limit is three, but I recognise that this leaves out Anderson's lipid-screening contribution, and I would like you and Sparr to say which of Hope, Madden or Anderson has the strongest claim on the ionizable-lipid concept itself.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept two nucleic-acid-medicine topics in one prize given overlap with the 2020 CRISPR and 2023 Medicine prizes
Credit split between the Vancouver and Boston lineages for lipid nanoparticles, and whether Hope or Anderson takes the third seat
Whether Liu alone, or Liu with Komor and Gaudelli, is the right attribution for base editing given Target-AID
Whether targeted protein degradation can be reduced to a single clean citation and three names
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I am at Lund University with committee colleagues Somfai and Sparr, but none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to Lund or to my own research group.
